opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes back to what we believe spatial intelligence is really for. When you generate a world in Marble, it's not meant to be a static postcard. It's a place, and places are meant to be moved through, experienced, and told stories in. Recording a scene is how creators turn that space into something they can share and build on.

If you talk to filmmakers, game designers, or architects, the world itself is just the starting point. What they need is to choreograph a camera through it, frame a shot, control the pacing, show someone a walkthrough. Before, you'd have to export to another tool or rebuild things by hand. Being able to move the camera and capture that path directly inside the world closes that loop and puts the creator in the director's chair.

There's also a deeper reason I care about. Because the world is 3D and consistent, a recorded path through it is *grounded*: objects stay where they are, geometry holds up, lighting behaves. That's very different from asking a model to hallucinate frames one after another and hoping they cohere. So recording isn't just a convenience. It shows why an explicit, persistent 3D representation matters. You get control and consistency, which is exactly what professional creative work demands.

And looking further ahead, those trajectories through a world are data. They're how you'd simulate an embodied agent's viewpoint, or generate training material for robotics, or prototype a VR experience. So something that looks like a simple feature today is part of a much bigger picture: worlds you can see, navigate, interact with, and eventually reason about.

r002.rationale: It says the world is 3D and consistent, but does not explain that precise camera placement requires a sense of three-dimensional space.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me start by saying that when we built Marble, the core ambition was never just to generate pretty 3D scenes. It was to build a world model, and a world model, by definition, has to deal with the world as it actually is, not just as we imagine it. Imagination is important, text-to-world and image-to-world are wonderful, but there's an enormous amount of value in the real, physical spaces that people live in, work in, build in.

So the ability to record a scene, to walk through a room or a construction site or a street with a phone or a camera and have Marble reconstruct that into a persistent, editable, navigable 3D world, that closes a loop I care about deeply. It connects the generative side of spatial intelligence to perception. For me, the whole arc of my career, from ImageNet onward, has been about machines seeing and understanding the physical world. Recording is where seeing meets creating.

And practically, it changes who the user is. A game designer can type a prompt and get something beautiful. But an architect, a robotics engineer, a filmmaker doing a location scout, a person who wants to preserve their grandmother's kitchen, they need the world they already have, captured faithfully, and then they need to be able to edit it, extend it, simulate in it. That's where generation and capture start to blend, where you can record half a space and let the model complete the rest with coherent geometry.

There's also a bigger reason. If we believe spatial intelligence is going to be as foundational as language, then the training signal matters. Real captured environments carry physics, scale, lighting, the messiness of actual rooms. Those are the things models get wrong when they only learn from synthetic or purely generated data. So recording is both a product feature and, honestly, part of how we think the whole field of world models gets better over time.

Recording that experience lets you capture a particular perspective, revisit it, and share it with someone else. So you’re taking something interactive and making it something you can communicate. For a creator, that’s a very useful bridge between exploring a world and telling a story within it.
